transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-15 10:00 AM PST (18:00Z)
Duration: ~65 minutes
Recording: Zoom (auto-transcript)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE); Priya Patel (Infra); Samir Khan (ML Lead, NovaDocs); Lena Ortiz (SRE, NovaDocs); Tom Evans (CTO, NovaDocs)
Shared: benchmark spreadsheet (drive link), onprem checklist (doc link), sample trace tar (s3 link)

Summary:
- Deep dive on a recent accuracy regression when running mixed quantization (INT8/AWQ/GPTQ) under onprem with intermittent network jitter.
- Hypothesis: KV-cache staleness + batching coalescing under SNAT/retry latency caused misaligned KV slots and subtle model attention drift for a subset of prompts.
- Action plan: run controlled layerwise sweeps, capture kernel selection logs, and reproduce jitter in lab with simulated packet delay.

Topics covered:
- quant formats: INT8 vs AWQ vs GPTQ vs FP8
- KV cache coherence and prefix staleness
- batching/coalescing heuristics and p99 tail effects
- kernel selection and compilation flags that affect numerical paths
- VPC/onprem network noise, SNAT and ephemeral port exhaustion impacts
- rollback/fallback strategies and runtime gating

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: okay uh thanks everyone for joining, quick agenda, go over the regression, what we saw in the onprem run, then triage steps. if we need more time we'll schedule follow-up.
[00:28] Samir Khan: thanks Maya, yeah we observed a drop in rouge/accuracy for about 7% of our testset after swapping to hybrid int8-awq to save cost. the overall tokens per second went up but some prompts returned hallucinated references, weirdly concentrated around long-prefix docs.
[01:10] Diego Alvarez: can you recall which model variant? was it the awq-quantized runtime or gptq post-quant?
[01:22] Samir Khan: it was the AWQ pipeline we put behind Redwood Dedicate — uh Redwood Dedicated onprem installer. we used AWQ by default but kept GPTQ snapshots for compare.
[01:40] Lena Ortiz: we also had a networking blip on 2026-11-29 around 03:12 UTC, SNAT logs show a flurry of retries and 200-500ms spikes for internal control plane calls.
[02:05] Priya Patel: that's interesting because the runtime logs show KV cache flush events and batch coalescer kicks around the same timestamps. there might be an interplay where prefix tokens were re-requested and KV pointers got re-assigned.
[02:33] Tom Evans: so are we saying the cache is getting stale and then the model gets different attention context? I'd expect the model to be deterministic but small alignment issues can cascade.
[02:50] Diego Alvarez: yeah small drift, especially with per-layer quantization differences, can change attention weights. AWQ's per-channel scale uses a different zero-point handling vs GPTQ, and when you combine cached KV slices compiled with different kernel flags we can get floating point rounding differences that amplify.
[03:15] Samir Khan: we didn't intentionally mix kernel compiled artifacts but our canary had a mix: some nodes had optimized kernels for fp16 and some the int8 paths. maybe the fallback path wasn't uniform.
[03:38] Maya Chen: right and the compilation/selection logic picks kernel by sequence length and hardware. if a request shifts from warm KV to cold fetch due to network retry, the runtime may pick a different kernel mid-sequence. that's risky.
[04:05] Lena Ortiz: we have the trace for the jitter window - i'll upload. it shows ephemeral port reuse and some control plane timeouts. that probably caused the redis-like KV store to miss a write briefly.
[04:28] Priya Patel: small misses in KV writes are usually recovered by prefix re-fetch, but with batching coalescing enabled the runtime sometimes collapses re-fetches into a single request that assumes compatible quantization layout. if the layout differs it's a mismatch.
[05:10] Diego Alvarez: to be explicit: mismatch vectors -> different dot products -> attention distribution shifts -> downstream tokens differ. it's a numeric sensitivity chain.
[05:35] Tom Evans: what about FP8? would fp8 avoid this because it's a different dynamic range?
[05:48] Diego Alvarez: FP8 can help for some models but it's not a panacea. FP8 path uses different kernels and rounding behavior; it may actually increase variance in very low-precision layers unless carefully calibrated. AWQ's integer-based approach can be more stable if layer statistics are well captured.
[06:20] Samir Khan: can we do a layerwise sweep to find offending layers? we have a subset of prompts that reproduce reliably.
[06:33] Diego Alvarez: yes. plan is: run int8-awq-gptq per-layer ablation on the failing prompts, record per-layer KL divergence and token-level edit distance. we suspect middle transformer layers (12-20 range) based on earlier runs.
[07:00] Maya Chen: logistical note—we'll need NovaDocs to run the sweep on a small onprem cluster or give us the model snapshot. for security we can run on our dedicated lab but we want to reproduce the same kernel/OS/hyperthread config.
[07:25] Samir Khan: we prefer you run in our environment; we'll provision a 2-node test cluster next week.
[07:40] Lena Ortiz: regarding observability, we need more fine-grained kernel selection logs and a timeline of KV cache offset IDs; current logs only show cache hit ratios.
[08:05] Priya Patel: we can add a small instrument that emits kernel-id and quant-profile id per request. that'll add low overhead.
[08:20] Tom Evans: what's the rollback strategy if we can't fix quickly? can we force runtime to use a single quant profile or degrade to fp16?
[08:33] Diego Alvarez: yes, runtime supports model pinning and quant-profile fencing. options: 1) pin to GPTQ full (fallback to slower but stable), 2) force FP16 for the few problematic layers, 3) enable strict kernel-coherence: disallow kernel switches mid-request, or 4) globally disable batching coalescer (costly).
[09:05] Samir Khan: cost-wise we prefer avoiding full fp16 but SLA matters. 9am product demo next month could be impacted.
[09:18] Maya Chen: let's prioritize reproducibility then remediation.

--- mid-call deep technical exchange ---
[18:02] Diego Alvarez: walked through example trace: request A starts on node 1 compiled with kernel-vec-7 (int8 path), during processing control plane hiccup causes reassign to node 2 where the compiled kernels come from a different build (quant profile id 17 vs 13). the KV offsets were identical but the decoded scale factors differed. we saw per-token logits shift by up to 0.6 in logit space.
[19:10] Priya Patel: we found a compiler flag -fast-math-toggle that changes fused-mul-add ordering; small but enough to change int8 dequantization rounding.
[20:00] Samir Khan: is that something Redwood's build system could lock down for onprem installs? we can't manage kernel flags across customer nodes easily.
[20:18] Maya Chen: yes we can provide a canonical onprem build bundle and a checksum validation routine to ensure all nodes run identical kernels. it's part of the onprem checklist.
[20:35] Tom Evans: good. but network noise still exists; how do we avoid cache staleness if a write is delayed?
[20:50] Diego Alvarez: approach: stronger KV write acks (wait-for-2 replicas), or versioned KV entries with per-request affinity so that nodes can detect stale prefixes and force recompile/convert before using them. both add latency.
[21:15] Lena Ortiz: increasing replication will add 10-20ms to tail, that may push us over p99 SLO. we need a middle ground.
[21:30] Priya Patel: runtime could sandbox the first N tokens after a cache refill with conservative fp16 fallback for those tokens to ensure alignment, then switch back. it's a gating technique we call warm-safe gating.
[22:00] Diego Alvarez: yes, warm-safe gating: for the first 8 tokens after a KV refill, force non-quantized or higher-precision compute, then resume. this avoids the cascade. cost impact small if cache hits are common.
[22:25] Samir Khan: sounds promising. do we have telemetry to measure how often refill events happen?
[22:38] Priya Patel: current metrics show 95% warm hits but refill spikes correlate with your jitter windows; we can add a counter and histogram.
[23:00] Maya Chen: action item: add kernel-id + quant-profile id + kv-version to trace, add warm-safe gating toggles to runtime, and run the layerwise sweep.

--- end of deep exchange, Q&A and recap ---
[57:12] Samir Khan: couple quick Qs — if we force single kernel id is there a perf hit on seq-len distribution? some of our workloads have long docs, others short.
[57:30] Diego Alvarez: yes there's a throughput tradeoff. forcing a single kernel optimized for long sequences will hurt short-sequence latency and vice versa. the runtime can pick per-route policies: for routes where accuracy-critical use mode A, for e.g. search use mode B.
[58:10] Lena Ortiz: about SSO/KMS integration—will the onprem bundle support customer-managed KMS/HSM?
[58:25] Maya Chen: yes, the onprem flow supports KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK, and HSM via PKCS#11) plus audit logs. I'll send the checklist.
[58:45] Tom Evans: and security review follow-up? we schedule with your security team next week?
[59:00] Maya Chen: yep, I'll coordinate.
